insider_note: 1/(1+x²) is the derivative of Tan⁻¹x — recognising THIS particular derivative, rather than a trig or log one, is what unlocks the substitution here.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute t = Tan⁻¹x
steps.why: d/dx[Tan⁻¹x] = 1/(1+x²), so the factor dx/(1+x²) converts directly to dt, leaving the outer sine of Tan⁻¹x as a plain sint.
common_mistakes: Not recognising 1/(1+x²) as the derivative of Tan⁻¹x, and trying a trig substitution x=tanθ instead (which also works but is far slower here).
Substituting t=x² or t=1+x² instead of t=Tan⁻¹x, which does not remove the sin(·) wrapper.
steps.memory_tip: 1/(1+x²) is the SIGNATURE derivative of Tan⁻¹x — spotting it instantly saves a much longer trig-substitution route.

steps.label: Integrate and back-substitute for the final answer
steps.why: ∫sint dt = −cost + c, and substituting t=Tan⁻¹x back in gives the final answer as a cosine of an inverse tangent.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the minus sign on ∫sint dt = −cost.
Forgetting to substitute Tan⁻¹x back in for t.
steps.memory_tip: ∫sint dt = −cost — the same sign rule as answer 149.1, now with Tan⁻¹x standing in for logx.
